title: The full bath
hookLine: a full wash after intimacy, after menstruation, before Friday and Eid

cards: Friday morning, early. The kettle's on, the kids are still asleep, and a father stands in the shower a little longer than usual. He isn't lingering.

He's working through an order: hands first, then the wudu he knows by heart, then water through the roots of his hair, then over his head, then over the whole body, right side, left side, until nothing is left dry.

Later he'll put on his good shirt and go to the Friday prayer. To anyone passing the bathroom door, it's just a shower. To him it has a name, and steps that come from a description kept in the hadith.

teach.b: The name is ghusl, the full bath. Where wudu washes certain limbs, ghusl reaches the whole body.
The Qur'an names it in the same verse that gives wudu, 5:6, and Pickthall's translation puts it simply: "And if ye are unclean, purify yourselves."
The fiqh books list when ghusl is required: after sexual intimacy, after a woman's menstruation ends, and after the bleeding that follows childbirth. Without it, the prayer waits.
Then there are times when it's recommended, a gift rather than a duty.
Before the Friday prayer: in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 877, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that whoever comes to the Friday prayer should bathe first.
Scholars discuss whether that wording makes it required or strongly recommended. And before the Eid prayers, which reports say companions of the Prophet ﷺ did. Now the steps.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 248, Aishah describes how he bathed.

He began by washing his hands. Then he made wudu as for prayer. Then he ran his fingers through the roots of his hair, poured three handfuls of water over his head, and let water flow over his whole body.

teach.h: AND IF YE ARE UNCLEAN, PURIFY YOURSELVES.
teach.b: That's the full sunnah form. Scholars explain that the minimum is less: the intention, and water reaching the whole body, with the schools differing on whether rinsing the mouth and nose belongs to that minimum.
So yes, a shower can be a ghusl. What turns it into one is the intention and the care that no part is skipped.

how: Muslims make ghusl, a full-body wash with intention, after intimacy and after menstruation or postnatal bleeding before praying again, and as a recommended bath before the Friday prayer and the Eid prayers, following the steps Aishah described.

games.q: you're about to make ghusl in the sunnah way Aishah described. what comes right after washing your hands?
o: wash the right side of your body.
games.why: in Bukhari 248 he washed his hands, then made wudu as for prayer, then ran wet fingers through his hair.

practice: Walk through the steps without water, slowly enough that you'd notice a missed spot: your hands washed, then the wudu limb by limb, fingers through the roots of your hair, water poured over your head, then running over your shoulders and back, down to your feet, right side, then left.
If you make ghusl, you can carry this order into your next one.

wordCard.voice: Ghusl. The full bath: required after intimacy and after menstruation, recommended before Friday and Eid, done with intention and nothing left dry. Today's word.
